text: Devil May Cry 3: Dante's Awakening is a 2005 action-adventure game developed and published by Capcom, serving as a prequel to the original Devil May Cry and featuring a younger Dante. Set a decade before the first game in an enchanted tower called the Temen-ni-gru, the story follows Dante as he tries to stop his twin brother, Vergil, from opening a portal to the Demon World. The game emphasizes combat mechanics centered on combos and fast-paced action, with the story primarily told through cutscenes using the game's engine and several pre-rendered full motion videos. Released in Japan on February 17, 2005, for the PlayStation 2, it launched in North America and other regions in February and March 2005. A Windows version was developed by SourceNext and released by Ubisoft on June 28, 2006, in Europe and October 16, 2006, in North America. The game received highly positive reviews, praised for its combat, level design, music, and characters, though some criticized its high difficulty in the North American release. A 2006 re-release, Devil May Cry 3: Special Edition, introduced retooled difficulty levels, mid-mission checkpoints, "GOLD mode," and made Vergil a playable character. The special edition also added a survival mode called "Bloody Palace" with 9,999 levels, a Jester fight early in the game (with optional later fights), "Turbo Mode" increasing game speed by 20 percent, an easier "continue" feature in GOLD mode, and rebalanced difficulty. Vergil's gameplay differs from Dante's; although Dante is weaker in skills and combos, he is easier to control. Due to space limitations, not all of Vergil's moves were included in the special edition. Vergil has a "Dark Slayer" style (similar to Dante's "Trickster"), which can be leveled up twice, and three weapons: Yamato (katana), Beowulf gauntlets and greaves, and the Force Edge broadsword. He has two attack ranges: "Summoned Swords" and "Judgment Cut." The game's original version begins with Dante's unnamed shop in the early 1990s, where a mysterious man, Arkham, arrives with an invitation from Vergil, leading to a demonic attack. After defeating demons, a tower erupts, and Dante interprets this as a challenge. He battles demons, some of which become his weapons, and is attacked by Mary, Arkham's daughter, who seeks revenge for her mother's death. It is revealed that Arkham works for Vergil and plans to use the amulet to connect the human and demonic worlds. After reaching the tower's summit and battling Vergil, who defeats Dante and steals his amulet, Dante's blood seals Rebellion, awakening his demonic powers. He is then swallowed by Leviathan, escapes, and later catches Vergil in the basement, where they fight again, interrupted by Mary and Jester. Jester reveals himself to be Arkham, who manipulates events to reactivate the tower and steal the Force Edge to rule a demon-infested Earth. The tower transforms, Arkham is carried to the summit, and Vergil disappears. Dante defeats Mary, gains her most powerful weapon, reaches the summit, crosses into the demonic world, and confronts Arkham, who transforms into a blob-like creature. Vergil reappears and they work together to expel Arkham, who lands on the tower where Mary finds and kills him, renouncing her name and calling herself Lady. In the demonic world, Dante and Vergil fight for the Force Edge and amulet halves; after Vergil's defeat, he vanishes with his half of the amulet. Dante meets Lady outside the tower, they become friends, and Dante names his shop "Devil May Cry." A post-credits scene shows Vergil in the demonic world, weak but determined, charging into battle against Mundus, a prequel to the first game. The game was developed as a return to form after the mixed reception of Devil May Cry 2, with a re-examination of gameplay elements like environment size and battle engine, and a return to the series' original tone, including Dante's cockiness and difficulty. The game's design focused on a battle system allowing stylish weapon control and a new in-game camera to maintain focus during battles. The Japanese release had lower difficulty than the North American and European versions, and Dante was portrayed as a younger, more arrogant character. The game was officially announced in PSM Magazine #85 in June 2004 and received a trailer at E3 on May 12, 2004, with a playable demo. Originally slated for a December 2004 release, it was pushed to February 2005 in Japan and March 2005 elsewhere. Capcom promoted the game with a multi-million dollar television campaign and extensive advertising, emphasizing its plot and fighting styles. The special edition was released on January 24, 2006, as part of the PlayStation 2 greatest hits collection, and later in Europe. Combined sales of both versions exceeded 2.3 million units, and the game has been cited as one of the greatest video games ever made. A 2005 manga prequel to the storyline was published in Japan and later in the United States. The gameplay includes levels and missions where players battle enemies, complete platforming tasks, and solve puzzles. Missions are graded from D to S and SS based on time, red orbs collected, stylish combat, item usage, and damage received. Stylish combat is tracked by an on-screen gauge that increases with uninterrupted attacks and damage avoidance, progressing from "Dope" to "Crazy," "Blast," "Alright," "Sweet," "SShowtime," and peaking at "SSStylish"; if damage is taken, the gauge falls and resets if at "Crazy" or below. The battle system allows linking attacks, with each weapon having a set number of attacks. Devil Trigger enables a demonic form that increases attack and defense, restores health, and allows special attacks, with the gauge filling by attacking or taunting and depleting when using the transformation. Dante gains access to Devil Trigger only one-third of the way through the game, while Vergil, playable in the special edition, has it from the start. The game features four combat styles: "Trickster" (dodging and agility), "Swordmaster" (sword and weapon techniques), "Gunslinger" (firearms), and "Royal Guard" (repelling attacks with a button press). Later, "Quicksilver" (slows enemies) and "Doppelgänger" (creates a shadow double, controllable by a second player) are unlocked. A two-player mode similar to Doppelgänger is available during Dante and Vergil's battle against Arkham. In the special edition, Vergil has the "Dark Slayer" style. The Nintendo Switch version of Devil May Cry 3: Special Edition added the ability to switch between combat styles at any point during combat. The Devil Trigger designs for Dante and Vergil were created by Kazuma Kaneko from Atlus, who previously worked on Zone of the Enders, Shin Megami Tensei III, and the Persona series. The Capcom staff praised Kaneko's work. In the original game, Vergil was intended to be alive, a decision made by Hideki Kamiya after Daigo Ikeno wanted to create an alternate universe where he survived, contrary to his earlier death in the first game. One of the key themes is familial conflict between Dante and Vergil. Morihashi wanted the scene where Lady kills Arkham, believing it emphasized the game's themes, and included a scene where Lady states Arkham is her responsibility to balance it. Dante appears bare-chested under his coat, a design meant to contrast with Vergil's fully clothed look and fit his youthful personality. Vergil is depicted with a Japanese katana and blue clothing, contrasting with Dante's red clothing and longsword Rebellion. The staff intended for the twins to share a hairstyle in the opening to confuse new players. The creation of Vergil's outfit posed challenges due to 3D movement, with staff joking he should remove his coat when fighting. Reuben Langdon provided Dante's voice and motion capture, auditioning four times before being chosen; he played his own version of the character and later said the role was one of the most difficult and rewarding of his career. When cast as Vergil, Southworth, who knew samurai culture, delivered a performance that matched the character's calm exterior and underlying rage. The staff found motion-capturing action scenes challenging but enjoyable. Vergil was made playable in the special edition due to extra development time, though some moves were removed due to space limitations. Vergil was designed to be stronger and harder to control than Dante, reflecting his calm personality. He became a favorite among the development team and was well received in the United States due to the popularity of katana-wielding characters in Hollywood films. After the game's release, Capcom introduced merchandise, including a manga by Suguro Chayamachi published by Tokyopop and a Dante action figure by Revoltech. A 2006 sourcebook, Devil May Cry 3 Material Archive - Note of Naught, included unreleased production art, storyboards, and a UMD video disc for the PSP (region 2 only). A three-disc soundtrack was released on March 31, 2005, produced by Tetsuya Shibata and Kento Hasegawa with lyrics and vocals by Shawn McPherson. At the 2005 Tokyo Game Show, Capcom announced the special edition. The original version sold 1.3 million copies, and the special edition sold 1 million units.

The 006 sourcebook, Devil May Cry 3 Material Archive - Note of Naught, featured previously unreleased production and CG artwork, storyboards, and a UMD video disc for the PSP with trailers and videos (region 2 only). A three-disc Devil May Cry 3 soundtrack was released on March 31, 2005, shortly after the game's release, produced by Tetsuya Shibata and Kento Hasegawa, with lyrics and vocals by Shawn McPherson. At the 2005 Tokyo Game Show, Capcom announced a special edition of Devil May Cry 3 with gameplay changes and additional content. The special edition was released on January 24, 2006, as part of the PlayStation 2 greatest hits collection, and it was later confirmed that the PlayStation 2 version would be released in Europe. Devil May Cry 3: Special Edition went on to sell 1 million units. On February 1, 2006, Ubisoft announced a Windows version of the game developed by SourceNext. The European PC version was the first released on June 28, 2006, before the special edition PlayStation 2 version in that region. The Japanese version was released two days later, and the North American version on October 16. Together with Devil May Cry and Devil May Cry 2, and Devil May Cry 3: Special Edition was re-released in the Devil May Cry HD Collection for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 on April 3, 2012. The HD collection was later released on PC, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One on March 13, 2018, with this iteration of Devil May Cry 3 sporting extra improvements over the original PC release, including XInput controller support. In 2020, Capcom rereleased the game for the Nintendo Switch. This edition is based on the Devil May Cry 3: Special Edition in the Devil May Cry HD Collection, with additional features such as allowing Dante to switch among all weapons and styles, just like in Devil May Cry 4 and Devil May Cry 5. It also adds the option to have local co-op in Bloody Palace mode using Dante and Vergil. Matt Walker was in charge of aiding the developers of this port of the game, seeking new ideas that might fit into it. The review aggregator website Metacritic gave the original PlayStation 2 release an 84 out of 100, and the Special Edition an 87 out of 100. It was included on Game Informer's list of the top 50 games of 2005, and the special edition received a "Game of the Month" award. In 2010, IGN ranked it 18th on its list of the top 100 PlayStation 2 games, and a GamePro retrospective that year rated it the 28th-best game for the PS2. Reviews typically praised the game for avoiding its predecessor's mistakes and for customization options, gameplay, combat engine, and the musical score despite the contradicting plot lines and character arcs. The style-based combat engine was considered to produce fighting sequences superior to games such as Ninja Gaiden and Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones, and the camera and controls were praised. Devil May Cry 3 was included in the 2010 book, 1001 Video Games You Must Play Before You Die. The high level of difficulty of the North American version of the initial release was criticized in otherwise-positive reviews. Critics disagreed with Capcom's decision to make the Japanese version's "hard" mode the North American "normal" mode, and the European version of Devil May Cry 3 had the same normal mode as the Japanese version, but maintained the yellow orb continue system of the North American version. The PC version was considered vastly inferior to the PlayStation 2 version due to the poor porting process. Issues included its game engine (thought rough and underpowered), its controls, and the inability to save the game and exit, a feature of most PC games. Jeremy Dunham of IGN gave the PC version a score of 5.8 out of 10 (compared to the PS2 version's 9.6), citing its "awful performance" and "craptacular controls". In 2021, PC Gamer listed the PC version as one of the worst PC ports. The special edition PlayStation 2 release ranked ninth on GameSpy's 2006 "Game of the Year" list; it was commended for recalibrating its difficulty, a survival mode known as "Bloody Palace" returning from the second game and making Vergil a playable character. Play as Vergil was cited for the character's difference from Dante, although the reuse of Dante's bosses and the lack of cutscenes was criticized.
